source_text: Ὅθεν καὶ ἐπιμένει ὁ θεὸς τὴν σύγχυσιν καὶ κατάλυσιν τοῦ παντὸς κόσμου μὴ ποιῆσαι, ἵνα καὶ οἱ φαῦλοι ἄγγελοι καὶ δαίμονες καὶ ἄνθρωποι μηκέτι ὦσι, διὰ τὸ σπέρμα τῶν Χριστιανῶν, ὃ γινώσκει ἐν τῇ φύσει ὅτι αἴτιόν ἐστιν. Ἐπεὶ εἰ μὴ τοῦτο ἦν, οὐκ ἂν οὐδὲ ὑμῖν ταῦτα ἔτι ποιεῖν καὶ ἐνεργεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν φαύλων δαιμόνων δυνατὸν ἦν, ἀλλὰ τὸ πῦρ τὸ τῆς κρίσεως κατελθὸν ἀνέδην πάντα διέκρινεν, ὡς καὶ πρότερον ὁ κατακλυσμὸς μηδένα λιπὼν ἀλλ᾿ ἢ τὸν μόνον σὺν τοῖς ἰδίοις παρ᾿ ἡμῖν καλούμενον Νῶε, παρ᾿ ὑμῖν δὲ Δευκαλίωνα, ἐξ οὗ πάλιν οἱ τοσοῦτοι γεγόνασιν, ὧν οἱ μὲν φαῦλοι, οἱ δὲ σπουδαῖοι. Οὕτω γὰρ ἡμεῖς τὴν ἐκπύρωσίν φαμεν γενήσεσθαι, ἀλλ᾿ οὐχ, ὡς οἱ Στωϊκοί, κατὰ τὸν τῆς εἰς ἄλληλα πάντων μεταβολῆς λόγον, ὃ αἴσχιστον ἐφάνη· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ καθ᾿ εἱμαρμένην πράττειν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἢ πάσχειν τὰ γινόμενα, ἀλλὰ κατὰ μὲν τὴν προαίρεσιν ἕκαστον κατορθοῦν ἢ ἁμαρτάνειν, καὶ κατὰ τὴν τῶν φαύλων δαιμόνων ἐνέργειαν τοὺς σπουδαίους, οἷον Σωκράτην καὶ τοὺς ὁμοίους, διώκεσθαι καὶ ἐν δεσμοῖς εἶναι, Σαρδανάπαλον δὲ καὶ Ἐπίκουρον καὶ τοὺς ὁμοίους ἐν ἀφθονίᾳ καὶ δόξῃ δοκεῖν εὐδαιμονεῖν. Ὃ μὴ νοήσαντες οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καθ᾿ εἱμαρμένης ἀνάγκην πάντα γίνεσθαι ἀπεφήναντο. Ἀλλ᾿ ὅτι αὐτεξούσιον τό τε τῶν ἀγγέλων γένος καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐποίησεν ὁ θεός, δικαίως ὑπὲρ ὦν ἂν πλημμελήσωσι τὴν τιμωρίαν ἐν αἰωνίῳ πυρὶ κομίσονται. Γενητοῦ δὲ παντὸς ἥδε ἡ φύσις, κακίας καὶ ἀρετῆς δεκτικὸν εἶναι· οὐ γὰρ ἂν ἦν ἐπαινετὸν οὐδὲν αὐτῶν, εἰ οὐκ ἂν ἐπ᾿ ἀμφότερα τρέπεσθαι καὶ δύναμιν εἶχε. Δεικνύουσι δὲ τοῦτο καὶ οἱ πανταχοῦ κατά λόγον τὸν ὀρθὸν νομοθετήσαντες καὶ φιλοσοφήσαντες ἄθρωποι ἐκ τοῦ ὑπαγορεύειν τάδε μὲν πράττειν, τῶνδε δὲ ἀπέχεσθαι. Καὶ σι῾ Στωϊκοὶ φιλόσοφοι ἐν τῷ περὶ ἠθῶν λόγῳ τὰ αὐτὰ τιμῶσι καρτερῶς, ὡς δηλοῦσθαι ἐν τῷ περὶ ἀρχῶν καὶ ἀσωμάτων λόγῳ οὐκ εὐοδοῦν αὐτούς. Εἴτε γὰρ καθ᾿ εἱμαρμένην φήσουσι τὰ γινόμενα πρὸς ἀνθρώπων γίνεσθαι, ἢ μηδὲν εἶναι θεὸν παρὰ τρεπόμενα καὶ ἀλλοιούμενα καὶ ἀναλυόμενα εἰς τὰ αὐτὰ ἀεί, φθαρτῶν μόνων φανήσονται κατάληψιν ἐσχηκέναι καὶ αὐτὸν θεὸν διά τε τῶν μερῶν καὶ διὰ τοῦ ὅλου ἐν πάσῃ κακίᾳ γινόμενον ἢ μηδὲν εἶναι κακίαν μηδ᾿ ἀρετήν· ὅπερ καὶ παρὰ πᾶσαν σώφρονα ἔννοιαν καὶ λόγον καὶ νοῦν ἐστι.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore God also remains to not make the confusion and dissolution of the whole world, so that also the evil angels and demons and humans may no longer be, because of the seed of the Christians, which He knows in nature that it is the cause. Since if this were not so, it would not be possible for you to still do and be energized by the evil demons, but the fire of judgment having come would have distinguished all, just as also previously the flood left no one except the one alone with his own, called Noah by us and Deucalion by you, from whom again so many have become, of whom some are evil and others are good. We say that the conflagration will come to be in this way, but not, as the Stoics, according to the reasoning of the change of all things into each other, which appeared most shameful; but neither do humans act or suffer what comes to be according to fate, but each one according to their own choice either does what is right or sins, and according to the energy of the evil demons the good people, such as Socrates and those like him, are persecuted and are in bonds, while Sardanapalus and Epicurus and those like them seem to be happy in abundance and glory. Which the Stoics, not understanding, declared that all things come to be according to fate and necessity. But that God made the beginning of the angels and humans to be self-determining, it is just that they will receive punishment in eternal fire for the things in which they sin. For the nature of all created things is to be receptive of evil and virtue; for nothing of theirs would be praiseworthy if it did not have the power to turn to both. And people who have legislated and philosophized everywhere according to the right reason show this, commanding some things to be done and others to be avoided. And even the Stoic philosophers, in their discourse on ethics, strongly honor the same things, as is clear in their discourse on principles and incorporeal things, which does not help them. For either they will say that the things that come to be happen to humans according to fate, or that there is no God except one that is changing and being altered and dissolved into the same things always, and they will appear to have grasped only perishable things, and God Himself, through both the parts and the whole, becomes in all evil or does not exist, and there is no evil or virtue; which is contrary to all sober thought and reason and mind.

pass_b_english: That is why God still refrains from bringing the confusion and dissolution of the entire world, so that the evil angels, demons, and human beings may not cease to exist, for the sake of the seed of the Christians, which He knows by nature is the cause. (Genesis 6–9) If this were not so, it would not be possible for you to go on doing these things and being energized by the evil demons; instead, the fire of judgment would have descended and separated everything completely, just as the flood once left no one alive except the one man with his family — called Noah by us and Deucalion by you — from whom so many have since been born, some evil and some good. We say the final conflagration will come in this way, but not as the Stoics teach, according to a theory of all things changing into one another, which is utterly shameful. Nor do we say that human beings act or suffer according to fate; rather, each person, by their own choice, either does what is right or sins. And because of the activity of evil demons, the good — people such as Socrates and those like him — are persecuted and put in chains, while men like Sardanapalus and Epicurus and their kind seem to flourish in abundance and glory. The Stoics, failing to understand this, declared that all things happen by fate and necessity. But because God made the very origin of both angels and humans self-determining, it is just that they will receive punishment in eternal fire for whatever they do wrong. For the nature of every created thing is to be capable of both vice and virtue; nothing in them would be praiseworthy if they did not have the power to turn toward either. This is shown by the people everywhere who have legislated and philosophized according to right reason, commanding certain things to be done and others to be avoided. Even the Stoic philosophers, in their ethical treatises, strongly honor the same virtues, yet their own treatises on first principles and incorporeal things undermine them. For either they will claim that what happens to human beings comes about by fate, or they will deny that there is any God other than one that is constantly changing, being altered, and dissolving into the same elements — and so they will appear to have grasped only perishable things, while God Himself, through both the parts and the whole, becomes the author of all evil or does not exist at all, and there is neither evil nor virtue — which is contrary to all sober thought, reason, and mind.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the distinction between the Stoic view of fate and the author's view of human choice (proairesis). Scripture citations (Genesis 6–9) are correctly added to the English text to identify the allusion to Noah and Deucalion. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.
